hints: Focus on the fact that the two esterification reactions share the same acid and the same water, so they are linked, not independent.
Write out the expressions for K1 and K2 and divide one by the other to see what cancels and what controls the ester ratio.
Consider what happens if you disturb only the second equilibrium by adding its ester, then follow where the extra acid and methanol must go.
walkthrough:
**Write both equilibrium expressions**

Think of the two reactions side by side. Both involve ethanoic acid and water.

$$K_1 = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}][\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}]}$$

$$K_2 = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}][\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}$$

**Divide to find the link between the esters**

Dividing cancels the common acid and water terms. This gives the key coupled relationship.

$$\frac{K_1}{K_2} = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3][\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3][\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}]}$$
Rearranged, the ester ratio depends on the alcohol ratio, not just on $K_1$ and $K_2$.

**Apply Le Chatelier to coupled equilibria**

If methyl ethanoate is added, $Q_2 > K_2$, so equilibrium 2 shifts left.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3(l) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}(l) + \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(l)$$

**Follow the extra acid through**

The left shift makes more ethanoic acid. That extra acid then disturbs equilibrium 1, making $Q_1 < K_1$, so equilibrium 1 shifts right to make more ethyl ethanoate.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}(l) + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3(l) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
Net effect: added methyl ester is partly converted, via acid, into ethyl ester.

options.A: Both alcohols can react with ethanoic acid, so both esters form. A much larger amount of ethanol means more ethyl ethanoate, but it does not prevent the small amount of methanol from reacting to give some methyl ethanoate.
options.B: Dividing K1 by K2 cancels $[H_2O]$ and $[CH_3CO_2H]$, but leaves the alcohols. The correct link is K1/K2 = ([ethyl][methanol])/([methyl][ethanol]), so [ethyl]/[methyl] = (K1/K2) x ([ethanol]/[methanol]). Option B wrongly omits the alcohol ratio.
options.C: Water appears in the numerator of both K1 and K2 to the same power, so it cancels in the ratio. Adding water shifts both hydrolyses to the left, decreasing both esters but leaving their mole ratio essentially unchanged.
options.D: Adding methyl ethanoate makes Q2 exceed K2, so the methyl equilibrium shifts left, producing ethanoic acid and methanol. The extra ethanoic acid then shifts the ethyl equilibrium to the right, increasing the moles of ethyl ethanoate. The two equilibria are coupled through the common acid.
